title: Dev log: testing 38 endings with zero playtesters as a two-person team
author: DepartmentPlus5191
selftext:
Hi again, it's Hop from Nibble & Hop.



In my last post I wrote about how we used AI to build our first game, and that AI got us to about 80% in every area. Today I want to write about a big part of that last 20% : testing.



Our game has 5 main endings and 33 bad endings. In a branching story, a broken branch usually doesn't crash anything. It just quietly locks the player out of an ending they'll never know existed. AI made writing the branching logic much faster, but it didn't make it any easier to trust. So we ended up putting more than 30% of our whole schedule into QA, walking through every path by hand.



We also tried recruiting public playtesters. Nobody applied. Not one person. Looking back, it makes sense, since no one knew who we were yet.



What saved us was a Korean streamer, Bbangttohwan, who played the game live in front of about 100 viewers. Watching someone play in real time and seeing chat react at the same moments showed us things we'd missed in our own testing, and we fixed several issues from that one stream. Other than that, it was just the two of us, a few internal testers and a small group of alpha testers.



We had also planned a demo early on, but the story runs as one continuous line, and every place we tried to cut it felt wrong. So we dropped the demo and decided to go straight to full release.



The feedback that made us happiest was about the bad endings. Players said they liked how some were dark and heavy while others were unexpectedly funny. That mix was exactly what Nibble & Hop had planned, so it was a relief to hear it actually worked.



If I had to sum up what I learned: AI speeds up making things, not checking them. If you're using AI heavily, budget real time for testing, and if you can't find playtesters, one stream can teach you a lot.



How do you all test branching stories? I'd love to hear if anyone has a good way to track every path.

comments.author: AriaTorres2
comments.body: For 38 endings, I'd keep a small test record for each: starting state, exact choices, expected ending ID, and build tested. That gives you a route to rerun after changes. I'd also add a near-miss case where a required flag is absent or a stat is just below its threshold. Reaching every ending won't catch one firing when it shouldn't. AI could help turn those choice sequences into replay tests, but I'd write the expected outcomes from the design notes rather than copy them from the generated logic.

replies.author: DepartmentPlus5191
replies.body: Unfortunately, this game does not end based on stats. But if it’s a game where your stats determine the ending, then I think I can definitely benefit from your suggestion. Thank you!
